name: spanish-basics

description.en: 120 basic Spanish words and phrases for beginners: the numbers 0–20, the tens and 100, the days of the week, the months, eight colours, family members, greetings and common phrases, and everyday nouns and verbs. The front shows the Spanish word, nouns with their article (el libro), except the days and months, whose gender is in a note; the back gives its English and Swedish meaning, or the digits for a number. Words, genders and meanings from Wikidata's lexemes and the US Foreign Service Institute's Spanish Basic Course (public domain), checked against the Real Academia Española's dictionary, Wiktionary and Folkets lexikon.
description.sv: 120 grundläggande spanska ord och fraser för nybörjare: talen 0–20, tiotalen och 100, veckodagarna, månaderna, åtta färger, familjemedlemmar, hälsningar och vanliga fraser samt vardagliga substantiv och verb. Framsidan visar det spanska ordet, substantiv med sin artikel (el libro) utom veckodagar och månader, vars genus står i en anteckning; baksidan ger betydelsen på engelska och svenska, eller siffrorna för ett tal. Ord, genus och betydelser från Wikidatas lexem och amerikanska Foreign Service Institutes Spanish Basic Course (fri från upphovsrätt), kontrollerade mot Real Academia Españolas ordbok, Wiktionary och Folkets lexikon.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Word list. A candidate list of 120 words for a first Spanish course was drawn up by hand from the brief's categories (numbers 0–20, the tens and 100; days; months; colours; family; greetings and phrases; everyday nouns; everyday verbs), choosing the most basic word for each concept and avoiding words whose everyday form differs between Spain and Latin America. No frequency list or textbook word list was copied.

Wikidata lexemes. The SPARQL query 1 fetched every Spanish lexeme (language Q1321) whose lemma is a candidate, with its category, gender (P5185), senses, glosses and sense items (P5137). Lemmas not found, or found without senses, were looked up with the lexeme search (API calls 2). The full JSON of the lexeme chosen for each word (the noun lexeme for nouns, the verb lexeme for verbs, and so on) was fetched with API calls 3, and the English and Swedish lexemes named by the senses' translation statements (P5972) with API calls 4. Feminine family words (hermana, hija, abuela) are forms of the lexemes hermano, hijo and abuelo, whose forms carry the feminine and singular features.

Wikidata items. The items linked from the senses (P5137) were fetched with API calls 5 and gave English and Swedish labels for days, months, colours, numbers and everyday things. For concepts with no item link (colours yellow, white, green and grey; brother, sister, woman, man, street, window, hand, work; greetings) items were found with the item search (API calls 6) and fetched with API calls 7.

Phrases. Wikidata has no Spanish lexeme for buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches, gracias, de nada, lo siento, hasta luego or mucho gusto. Their Spanish form and meaning were taken from the basic sentences of Units 1 and 2 of the Foreign Service Institute's Spanish Basic Course (1961, a US Government work in the public domain), read in the Internet Archive's OCR text (calls 10 and 11) and compared with the scanned layout of the English and Spanish columns. The English on the cards is our own choice of the usual English equivalent of that meaning, not always FSI's wording: FSI has "So long" (card: see you later), "Glad to meet you" (nice to meet you), "thanks" (thank you), "Good evening" (good evening, good night, the second added from RAE's "al irse a acostar") and "I'm very sorry" for Lo siento mucho (I'm sorry). These English backs are also the first glosses in English Wiktionary, which was consulted (step 8); they are short stock phrases, not protectable expression.

Writing the cards. The front is the Spanish word as in the lexeme's lemma (or form), nouns preceded by the definite article that matches their gender (el agua takes el although feminine). The back is our own short English and Swedish rendering of the main sense: for nouns the bare noun, for verbs the infinitive (English "to …", Swedish "att …"), for numbers the digits (untagged, since digits have no language). English and Swedish follow the Wikidata labels where an item exists; otherwise they are the standard Swedish equivalent, chosen by the authors and checked in Folkets lexikon (step 8). For the greetings and phrases, por favor and abuelo/abuela, where no CC0 source gives Swedish, the Swedish on the card is the same as the Folkets entry it was checked against (for example good morning → god morgon, pleased to meet you → trevligt att träffas, grandfather → farfar, morfar); these are single words or fixed greetings, facts of usage rather than protectable expression, and no Folkets definitions, examples or selection were used. Swedish uses lower case for days and months. Where one English word maps to two Swedish words (ir: gå or åka; vivir: leva or bo; abuelo: farfar or morfar) both are given.

Notes. A short note was added where it helps a beginner and is confirmed by the dictionary: irregular genders (el agua, la mano, el día), the gender of every day and month, the short form un, cien as the short form of ciento used for 100 by itself and before a noun, mil or millones (101–199 use ciento), the plural padres (parents), mujer also meaning wife, querer also meaning to love, sí versus si, ser versus estar (with ser for where an event takes place), naranja the colour versus la naranja the fruit (with a front note "colour"), noche also covering the evening after dark (buenas noches), lo siento also used in sympathy, Swedish requests often ending with tack rather than a word for please, the Swedish gå/åka distinction, buenos días being said until midday or lunch, and buenas tardes being used until nightfall. Notes are our own wording.

Cross-checking. Every Spanish word was looked up in the Real Academia Española's Diccionario de la lengua española (calls 12): its spelling, its grammatical gender against the article on the card, and its first relevant definition (quoted in each card's evidence). Every English meaning was checked against the Spanish section of the English Wiktionary (calls 13). Every Swedish word was checked in Folkets lexikon (calls 14), English → Swedish, or Swedish → English when the first direction had no match. Where the FSI vocabulary appendix lists the word, its English gloss was compared as well. A Python script built the evidence lines from the responses saved during authoring, so each quote is what the source returned (the look-up logic is recorded with calls 11–14); the raw responses and scripts were working files and are not published. Quotations from the RAE dictionary are cut to the headword, the grammatical label and the first words of the sense, marked with "…".

Machine checks. The dossier's Wikidata checks (the Spanish, English and Swedish label or alias of each linked item that matches the card's text, and the multilingual digit label of each number) are re-run against live Wikidata by the builder on every build. Wikidata lexemes cannot be checked by the builder (it checks items only); the lexeme facts in the evidence were read from the API responses of 4 October 2026.

Excluded: words whose usual form differs by region (car: coche/carro/auto; brown: marrón/café; juice: zumo/jugo; computer: ordenador/computadora), saber/conocer (both "to know", which needs more context than a flashcard gives), niño (child or boy), the morning/tomorrow pair mañana, and tiempo (time or weather), since each would need more than one answer.

Review rounds. Three independent AI reviewers (factual accuracy; language and translation; licensing and documentation) checked the deck, followed by two final re-check reviewers who re-checked the changed cards, every third card, the metadata and the documentation, and a final full-deck reviewer. Their findings were verified against the sources before any change: the Folkets entries sorry, ledsen, beklaga and wife, the RAE entries ser (acepción 7), día, mañana, tarde and anochecer, the FSI basic sentences for querer and ver (calls 15–17), and the Swedish Wiktionary entries buenos días, buenas tardes and naranja (call 18); in the re-checks, the mul labels of the number items (call 19), the English Wiktionary usage notes of cien (call 20) and the sense items of the lexemes hijo and abuelo (call 21). The resulting changes are listed under quality control, rounds 1–6.
selection: 120 cards: the cardinal numbers 0–20, the tens 30–90 and 100 (29); the seven days of the week; the twelve months; eight colours (red, blue, green, yellow, black, white, grey, orange); eight family members (mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, grandfather, grandmother); twelve greetings and common phrases; 25 everyday nouns (house, water, bread, milk, apple, book, table, chair, door, window, dog, cat, city, street, school, man, woman, friend, money, work, hand, day, night, year, week); and 19 common verbs in the infinitive (ser, estar, tener, hacer, ir, venir, hablar, comer, beber, vivir, querer, poder, ver, decir, escribir, leer, dormir, trabajar, comprar). The list was chosen by the deck's authors for a first course, not copied from any frequency list or textbook. Every word has a Wikidata lexeme except the eight phrases noted in the method, which come from the public-domain FSI course. Left out: words whose everyday form differs between Spain and Latin America (coche/carro, marrón/café, zumo/jugo, ordenador/computadora), word pairs a beginner cannot tell apart on a single card without context (saber/conocer), words with two equally common meanings (mañana, tiempo, niño), and brown and purple (several competing words). Colours are given in the masculine singular; the feminine form is in a note. Days and months are given without an article, as they are usually written; their gender is in a note on every day and month card.

rounds.scope: All 120 cards: every Spanish form, gender, English and Swedish meaning and note against the content sources and the three verification sources; the builder's Wikidata checks.
rounds.summary: Every card has evidence from a content source (Wikidata or the FSI course) and at least two of the verification sources; RAE, Wiktionary and Folkets agree with every card as written. The genders on the cards (article el or la) match the RAE entries for all 33 nouns and the Wikidata lexemes wherever the lexeme records a gender. The builder's Wikidata checks cover the Spanish, English and Swedish labels or aliases of 93 linked items (245 checks) and the digit label of every number; they all pass. Discrepancies between sources and how they were resolved are listed below.

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label for day (Q573) is "dygn" (a 24-hour period), not "dag".
findings.resolution: Kept "dag", the everyday word covering both senses of día, confirmed by Folkets lexikon (day → dag). The Swedish label check for Q573 was not added.

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish labels for grandfather and grandmother (Q9238344, Q9235758) are the descriptive "förälders far" and "förälders mor"; Swedish has no single neutral word.
findings.resolution: The cards give "farfar eller morfar" and "farmor eller mormor", as Folkets lexikon translates grandfather and grandmother. No Swedish label check for these items.

findings.issue: Wikidata lexeme L565768 (cuarenta) has grammatical gender feminine, while the other number lexemes are masculine and the RAE treats numbers used as nouns as masculine.
findings.resolution: The number cards show no article, so the card is unaffected; the discrepancy is recorded here for Wikidata's editors.

findings.issue: The Wikidata lexemes for amigo (L230374) and noche (L57895) record no grammatical gender.
findings.resolution: The article comes from the RAE entries ("amigo, ga", noche "f.") and, for noche, from FSI's feminine "Buenas noches"; both are facts, not copied text.

findings.issue: The item for man (Q8441) has the Spanish label "varón"; "hombre" is an alias.
findings.resolution: The check uses the alias; RAE acepción 3 ("Varón que ha llegado a la edad adulta") and Wiktionary ("man (adult male human)") confirm the meaning.

findings.issue: FSI renders Buenas noches as "Good evening"; Wiktionary gives both good evening and good night; RAE says it is used "durante la noche o al irse a acostar".
findings.resolution: The back gives both: good evening, good night / god kväll, god natt.

findings.issue: Wiktionary also gives "good evening" for buenas tardes.
findings.resolution: Kept good afternoon (FSI, Wikidata Q19279334) and added a note that la tarde runs from midday until nightfall (RAE tarde, acepción 1).

findings.issue: Swedish has no exact equivalent of please; Folkets lexikon lists varsågod, tack, ja tack, snälla.
findings.resolution: The back gives snälla, with a note that Swedish requests usually end with tack.

findings.issue: Folkets lexikon's English–Swedish entry for September has the misspelt translation "septembere", and its entries for yellow give only derived senses (gulna, feg).
findings.resolution: Checked in the Swedish–English direction instead (september → September, gul → yellow).

findings.issue: Both verbs are "to be" / "att vara", so the backs are not unique.
findings.resolution: Each has a note on when it is used. The deck is studied front to back only, so a back never has to identify one of the two.

findings.issue: The item first found for work, Q6958747, is a redirect to Q268378, so the builder's label checks against Q6958747 failed (the query service has no labels on a redirect).

findings.issue: The FSI course teaches Latin American Spanish.
findings.resolution: Only words and phrases that are standard everywhere were kept; each is in the RAE dictionary without a regional mark in the sense used.
